nameStory: Robinson's hawkweed is named after botanist Benjamin Lincoln Robinson, who helped identify many northeastern plants in the early 1900s. The 'hawkweed' part of the name comes from an old belief that hawks ate these plants to sharpen their eyesight - though that's just folklore, not fact!
description: Robinson's hawkweed is a small, delicate wildflower that rarely grows taller than your knee - usually reaching just 14 inches at most. It produces cheerful yellow daisy-like flowers on slender stems, with leaves arranged both in a low rosette at the base and scattered along the stem. This little-known member of the sunflower family has star-shaped hairs covering its parts and creates small clusters of 1-10 bright yellow flower heads. It's one of New England's rarest wildflowers, with only a handful of known locations.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flower heads with 30-50 thin ray petals arranged like a daisy, but no center disc flowers - just the outer yellow rays. The flowers form small flat-topped clusters of 1-10 heads per stem.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves up to 3 inches long arranged both in a basal rosette and scattered along the stem. Feel smooth on top with few hairs, but flip them over and you'll find dense, soft hairs on the undersides.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A small herb that stays quite short, rarely exceeding 14 inches tall. The plant has a compact, delicate appearance with slender stems rising from a leafy base.

idTips.label: Hairs
idTips.description: Look closely and you'll see distinctive star-shaped hairs covering the plant parts - these tiny stellar hairs feel soft to the touch and catch the light beautifully.

habitat: Robinson's hawkweed grows in the cooler regions of northern New England, particularly in Maine and New Hampshire, extending into eastern Canada. Look for it in open woodlands, forest edges, and clearings with well-drained soils. It prefers areas with partial shade to full sun and seems to favor slightly acidic soils typical of New England's coniferous and mixed forests.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in the basal rosette, with the soft star-shaped hairs becoming visible on fresh growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period when the cheerful yellow flower heads open in their flat-topped clusters. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seeds develop, while leaves may begin to yellow. The basal rosette often persists.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground parts die back, though some basal leaves may persist under snow cover in protected locations.

funFact: Robinson's hawkweed is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only twice in recent botanical surveys - making it rarer than finding a four-leaf clover, which occurs about once in every 5,000 plants!
confusionNotes: Robinson's hawkweed can be confused with other yellow hawkweeds, but its small size (under 14 inches), star-shaped hairs, and the specific combination of smooth upper leaf surfaces with hairy undersides help distinguish it. The flat-topped flower arrangement and lack of center disc flowers also set it apart from true sunflowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called Robinson's hawkweed after an American botanist, this species actually extends into eastern Canada and represents the interesting cross-border flora of the northern New England region. The hawkweed genus is notoriously difficult to identify, with many species hybridizing and showing subtle differences.
compareHints: Among its hawkweed relatives, Robinson's hawkweed stays much smaller than New England hawkweed or Canada hawkweed, which can grow much taller. Unlike rattlesnakeweed with its distinctive purple-veined leaves, Robinson's hawkweed has plain green foliage. The star-shaped hairs and small stature distinguish it from the more common spotted hawkweed, which has different hair types and often shows leaf spots.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Panicled hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by being much taller and more upright than species like rattlesnakeweed or spotted hawkweed.
Among its hawkweed relatives, rattlesnakeweed stands out for its ground-hugging rosette growth pattern and prominent leaf veining.
Rough hawkweed is much more bristly and hairy than its relatives like panicled hawkweed or Canada hawkweed, which have smoother stems and leaves.
Among the many hawkweed species in New England, common hawkweed is distinguished by its branching growth habit and grayish, hairy leaves.
Among New England's hawkweeds, this species stands out for its multi-branched flowering stems and medium height.
Among New England hawkweeds, Canada hawkweed stands out for its exceptionally narrow, smooth leaves and tall, elegant stature.
Among New England's hawkweeds, spotted hawkweed stands out for its tall, branching flower stems and tendency to grow in disturbed soils.
Among New England's hawkweeds, wall hawkweed is distinguished by its preference for rocky, vertical surfaces and its distinctly heart-shaped leaves with purple veining.
Among New England's hawkweeds, Beaked Hawkweed stands out for its extremely small flowers and very hairy lower stem.
